seo_title: Residential vs Commercial Insurance Appraisal in Texas
meta_description: Residential vs commercial insurance appraisal: how the process differs in scale, experts, timelines and business interruption. A guide for Texas owners.
h1: Residential vs Commercial Insurance Appraisal: Key Differences Explained
excerpt: How does residential vs commercial insurance appraisal differ? Compare scale, experts, business interruption, deductibles and timelines, plus what Texas owners should know.
key_takeaways: Residential and commercial appraisals follow the same basic appraisal clause process.
Commercial appraisals involve more buildings, experts and documentation.
Business interruption disputes often accompany commercial property claims.
Choose an appraiser and umpire with experience matching your property type.
Appraisal resolves amount-of-loss disputes, not coverage denials.
body_html:
Residential vs commercial insurance appraisal follows the same basic process: each side names an appraiser, an umpire resolves disagreements, and the panel sets the amount of loss. The differences are scale and complexity. Commercial appraisals involve more buildings, specialized systems, engineering input, tenants and sometimes business interruption, so they typically take longer and require more documentation.

What is insurance appraisal?

Insurance appraisal is a dispute resolution process written into most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies. It applies when the insured and the insurer agree the loss is covered but disagree on the amount. Either side can demand appraisal in writing.

The steps are generally the same for both property types:

  1. A written appraisal demand is sent under the policy's appraisal clause.
  2. Each party selects a competent, disinterested appraiser.
  3. The appraisers choose an umpire, or ask a court to appoint one if they cannot agree.
  4. The appraisers inspect, exchange estimates and try to agree item by item.
  5. The umpire decides any items still in dispute.
  6. An award signed by two of the three sets the amount of loss.

Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), Texas appraisers decide the amount of loss and may evaluate damage and causation related to that amount, but they do not decide coverage. For the fundamentals, read what is an insurance appraisal. This is general information, not legal advice.

Appraisal commonly resolves disputes over roof damage, water losses, fire claims, storm damage, underpaid estimates and scope disagreements, whether the property is a house or a shopping center.

Residential insurance appraisal explained

Residential appraisal covers single-family homes, townhomes, condominiums (for the unit owner's portion) and duplexes. Most disputes involve a focused set of damage:

Damage typeCommon causeTypical dispute
Roof damageHail and windRepair vs full replacement
Water intrusionStorm openings or pipe leaksExtent of affected areas
Fire and smokeElectrical or cooking firesCleaning vs replacement
Interior damageRoof leaks after stormsMatching of finishes
Structural damageFallen trees, severe weatherScope of framing repairs

Why residential appraisal usually moves faster

A typical home has one roof, one set of interior finishes and a manageable number of rooms. Appraisers can often inspect in a single visit, and estimates may be a few dozen pages. Disputes usually center on a handful of issues:

  • Roofing materials and whether a full replacement is needed
  • Interior finishes and matching
  • Labor pricing and overhead and profit
  • Moisture damage behind walls or under floors
  • Code upgrade requirements

Condominium unit owners are a special case. The association's master policy usually covers the building structure and common areas, while the unit owner's policy covers interior finishes and improvements. A residential appraisal on a condo claim may involve only the unit owner's portion, with the association's claim handled separately.

Many residential appraisals resolve within a few months, though timelines vary. See how long does an insurance appraisal take for what affects the schedule.

Residential policies in Texas

Texas homeowners policies come in several forms, and many carriers use their own versions. Most include an appraisal clause, along with features that often drive disputes, such as percentage wind/hail deductibles, roof ACV or payment schedule endorsements and cosmetic damage exclusions for metal roofing.

Commercial insurance appraisal explained

Commercial appraisal operates on a different scale. The claim may involve:

  • Office buildings
  • Shopping centers and retail strips
  • Apartment complexes
  • Warehouses and industrial facilities
  • Hotels
  • Churches, schools and medical buildings

A single claim may span multiple buildings, large low-slope roofs, rooftop HVAC equipment, storefront glass, specialty finishes and tenant improvements. For a multi-family example, see apartment complex insurance appraisal.

Why commercial claims become more complex

Commercial disputes frequently involve outside experts and documents that residential claims rarely need:

  • Engineering reports on roofs, structures or building envelopes
  • Roofing consultants, moisture surveys and core samples
  • Structural evaluations
  • Tenant improvement records and lease obligations
  • Code compliance reviews and permit requirements
  • Financial records for business income claims

Because quantities are so large, small differences in unit price, waste or scope multiply quickly. A difference of a few dollars per square on a large commercial roof can add up to a substantial amount.

Commercial roofs change the inspection

Many commercial buildings have low-slope membrane roofs where the most expensive damage, such as wet insulation and fractured cover board, sits beneath the surface. Appraisers often rely on infrared scans, moisture surveys and core samples to establish the scope. Residential appraisals rarely need that level of testing, which is one reason commercial timelines run longer.

Mixed-use and small commercial properties

Not every commercial claim is a large loss. A small retail building, a duplex held as a rental or a ground-floor shop with apartments above can sit between the two categories. These properties are usually insured on commercial forms, so expect commercial deductibles and possibly business income or loss of rents issues, but the damage itself may look a lot like a residential claim. The appraisal approach should match the policy and the property, not just the label.

How business interruption complicates commercial appraisal

When a commercial property is damaged, the owner may lose income as well as property. Business income or business interruption coverage is designed to replace that lost income during the period of restoration. Disputes may involve:

  • Lost revenue and how to calculate it
  • Payroll continuation
  • Temporary relocation and extra expenses
  • Inventory losses
  • Equipment downtime
  • Lease obligations and rent abatement
  • How long restoration should reasonably take

Whether these amounts fall within the appraisal clause depends on policy wording and the nature of the dispute. Some panels address property damage only, while others handle income loss as well. Learn more in business interruption vs property damage claims.

Tip: Commercial owners should start a separate file for income records the day of the loss: sales reports, payroll, rent rolls and extra expense receipts. Reconstructing them later is slow and invites disputes.

Choosing the right appraiser for each type of claim

Any appraiser should be competent and disinterested, but the right experience differs by property type.

For residential claims

  • Deep knowledge of residential roofing, interiors and local pricing
  • Clear, detailed Xactimate or Symbility estimates
  • Ability to explain matching, code and repair-versus-replace issues simply

For commercial claims

  • Experience with low-slope roofing, rooftop equipment and building envelopes
  • Capacity to document many buildings and large quantities efficiently
  • Comfort working alongside engineers and consultants
  • Organized presentation of evidence to the umpire

The umpire matters too, especially on commercial losses where disputed items carry large dollar values. Read about our insurance umpire services and our guide to commercial property insurance appraisal in Texas.

Residential and commercial appraisal in Texas

Texas property owners of every kind face hail across North and Central Texas, hurricanes along the Gulf Coast, freeze events that burst pipes statewide and wildfire risk in drier regions. Residential neighborhoods and commercial corridors in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, San Antonio and Austin often file claims from the same storm.

A few Texas rules apply to both:

  • Prompt payment: Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542 generally requires insurers to acknowledge a claim within 15 days, accept or reject it within 15 business days of receiving requested items and pay within 5 business days after acceptance.
  • Weather claim notice: Chapter 542A generally requires 61 days' written notice before suing over a weather-related claim.
  • After an award: the Texas Supreme Court's 2019 decisions in Barbara Technologies and Ortiz address how paying an appraisal award affects later prompt payment and extra-contractual claims.

Is appraisal worth it for your property?

Appraisal costs money: each side typically pays its own appraiser and splits the umpire's fee. On a residential claim, the amount in dispute needs to justify those costs. On a commercial claim, the stakes are often larger, but so is the effort. Our appraisal cost calculator helps you compare likely costs with the amount in dispute.

Residential owners should also consider the time involved. A homeowner may need to schedule inspections, gather records and wait for the panel to finish. Commercial owners face the same demands at a larger scale, often with tenants and lenders asking for updates along the way. In either residential vs commercial insurance appraisal, preparation is what keeps the process efficient.

Appraisal is usually the right tool when coverage is accepted, the disagreement is about scope or price, and negotiation has stalled. It is not designed to resolve outright coverage denials.

Next steps

Whether you own a single home or a portfolio of commercial buildings, the residential vs commercial insurance appraisal decision starts the same way: understand your appraisal clause, document the damage thoroughly and compare the carrier's estimate against a detailed independent estimate. The bigger and more complex the property, the earlier you should organize evidence and bring in experienced help.

faqs.q: Is the appraisal clause the same in homeowners and commercial policies?
faqs.a: The basic structure is similar: each side names an appraiser, an umpire resolves disagreements and an award signed by two of the three sets the amount of loss. Wording varies by carrier and form, including deadlines, appraiser qualifications and what the panel may address. Always read the appraisal clause in your specific policy.

faqs.q: Does commercial appraisal take longer than residential?
faqs.a: Usually. Commercial claims often involve multiple buildings, large roofs, engineering reports and business income questions, which add inspection and review time. Residential appraisals tend to involve one structure and fewer disputed items. Actual timelines depend on the size of the gap, the documentation and how responsive the appraisers are.

faqs.q: Can a homeowner use the same appraiser as a business owner?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the appraiser is competent and disinterested and has the right experience. Some appraisers handle both residential and commercial claims. For commercial losses, look for experience with low-slope roofing, rooftop equipment, multiple structures and working alongside engineers and consultants.

faqs.q: Does appraisal cover business interruption claims?
faqs.a: It depends on the policy language and the nature of the dispute. Some appraisal clauses apply to any amount of loss, which may include business income, while others are interpreted more narrowly. Commercial owners should review their policy and get advice before assuming income loss will be included.

faqs.q: How much does insurance appraisal cost?
faqs.a: Each side generally pays its own appraiser and splits the umpire's fee, though policy wording controls. Fee arrangements vary and may be hourly, flat or percentage based. Compare the likely cost with the amount in dispute before invoking appraisal, especially on smaller residential claims.
